notes:
I could do very little research for Isaiah 41, so these notes are mostly incomplete. The research tool hit its usage limit after a few early calls failed, and I couldn't search or open any more pages. The only commentary text I actually read was a short summary at the top of the Enduring Word page. Following your rules, I've noted only what that summary says and left out everything else.

**What I found (Enduring Word, David Guzik), https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/isaiah-41/**

- **Whole chapter:** Guzik reads the chapter as a courtroom scene. God calls the far-off nations and their idols to come and defend themselves. The nations see God's power and fear it, but then turn to making their own gods. Israel, by contrast, is called to trust the God who rules history and holds their hand. He stresses the repeated "fear not" and the many "I will" promises, which show God's plentiful resources, unshakeable power and constant love for His people.
- **vv. 2–4:** Commentators disagree about who "the one from the east" in v. 2 is: Abraham or Cyrus. Either way, Guzik says, the point is that God knows both the past and the future, while the idols know neither.
- **v. 4:** God calls Himself "the first and the last." Guzik says this gives Him authority over all of history, and it is what backs up the promise in v. 13.
- **vv. 5–7:** Guzik sees irony here. The nations react to God's power by helping each other build idols. The summary doesn't spell out the details.
- **vv. 10–13:** God's help is with His people now, so they need not fear. The promise in v. 13 that He will hold Israel's right hand rests on who He is, the first and the last (v. 4).

**What's missing**
- **Part 1:** I couldn't read the full Enduring Word page or Gill, Ellicott, the Pulpit Commentary or Precept Austin. So there are no notes yet for vv. 1, 3, 8–9, 11–12 or 14–29.
- **Part 2:** I found no material on where Protestant traditions disagree.
- **Part 3:** I found nothing from modern scholarship, Catholic or Orthodox sources, or on debated popular teaching.

These pages showed up in search results, but I couldn't read their content, so I've drawn nothing from them:
- Gill's commentary on Isaiah 41: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/isaiah-41.html
- Bible Hub commentaries on 41:2, which collect several older commentaries: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/isaiah/41-2.htm
- NET Bible Isaiah 41, which has translators' notes: https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Isa&chapter=41
- Precept Austin's Isaiah index: https://www.preceptaustin.org/isaiah_commentaries

If you ask again in a new turn, I can start by reading those pages in full. After that I'd look up Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary verse by verse on Bible Hub, then Catholic and Reformed or Lutheran sources on the Cyrus/Abraham question in v. 2 and on "worm Jacob" in v. 14.
